**What is Skin Cancer?**

Skin cancer is the most common form of cancer in the United States. According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), over 100,000 new cases of melanoma will be diagnosed this year, and over 8,000 people will die from the disease [1]. Melanoma skin cancer occurs much less often than the nonmelanoma skin cancers, but causes more deaths.

**Types of Skin Cancer**

There are two main categories of skin cancer: nonmelanoma skin cancer (NMSC) and melanoma. Nonmelanoma skin cancer is further divided into basal cell carcinoma (BCC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and other subtypes [2].

* Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC): BCC is the most common form of NMSC, accounting for about 75% of all skin cancers. It typically appears as a small, painless bump or mole on the skin that can be felt during a self-examination.
* Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC): SCC accounts for about 25% of NMSC cases and is more common in people who have had previous skin cancer or sunburned areas of their skin [3].
* Melanoma: Melanoma is the most serious form of skin cancer, accounting for about 5-10% of all NMSC cases. It can appear as a new mole or change an existing one.

**Causes and Risk Factors**

Skin cancer occurs when errors (mutations) occur in the DNA of skin cells. The mutations cause the cells to grow out of control and form a mass of cancer cells [4]. The main risk factors for skin cancer include:

* Exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun or tanning beds
* Fair skin, light hair, and light eyes
* Family history of skin cancer
* Previous skin cancer

**Symptoms**

The symptoms of skin cancer can vary depending on the type and location of the tumor. Common symptoms include:

* A new mole or change in an existing one
* A sore or blister that doesn't heal
* A bump or growth on the skin
* Redness, itching, or pain around the affected area

**Diagnosis and Treatment**

Early detection is crucial for successful treatment of skin cancer. The best way to find skin cancer before it becomes a serious problem is by checking your skin regularly [5]. If you notice any changes in your skin, see a doctor for a thorough examination.

Treatment options for skin cancer depend on the type and location of the tumor. These include:

* Surgery: Surgery is usually the most effective treatment option for early-stage skin cancers.
* Radiation therapy: Radiation therapy can be used to treat skin cancers that are too far advanced to surgery.
* Chemotherapy: Chemotherapy may be used to treat skin cancers that have spread to other parts of the body.
